subject: Cognitive Science
title: Signal Detection Theory
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Signal Detection Theory.

hook.text: A radar operator sees a blip. Is it an enemy plane or noise? The answer depends on more than the signal itself.

buildup.text: Signal detection theory separates sensitivity (how well you detect) from criterion (how willing you are to say 'yes').

discovery.text: Four outcomes exist: hit, miss, false alarm, and correct rejection. The tradeoff between them defines your strategy.

twist.text: Changing the payoff changes the criterion. If missing a cancer is worse than a false alarm, radiologists lower the bar.

climax.text: SDT applies everywhere: spam filters, airport security, medical screening—any decision under uncertainty.

punchline.text: Detection isn't just about seeing—it's about deciding.

quiz.question: What two factors does signal detection theory separate?

details.summary: Signal detection theory separates two aspects of perception: sensitivity, the ability to distinguish signal from noise, and criterion, the threshold you set for saying you detected something.
details.whyItMatters: Signal detection theory transformed psychology by showing that perception is not just about sensitivity but also about the decision criterion you adopt.
takeaways: Perception involves both sensitivity and decision criterion
Context and consequences shift the detection threshold
Hits, misses, false alarms, and correct rejections are all outcomes

faq.question: How do consequences affect detection criterion?
faq.answer: If missing a signal is costly, like a radiologist missing a tumor, you adopt a liberal criterion: report anything suspicious. More hits but also more false alarms. If false alarms are costly, like a jury convicting an innocent person, you adopt a conservative criterion.

faq.question: How is signal detection theory used in practice?
faq.answer: It is used in radiology to optimize diagnostic accuracy, in sonar operation to set alert thresholds, in quality control to balance defect detection against false rejects, and in memory research to separate genuine recognition from guessing bias.
